analogy.p: Think of GPE as how high up a hill you are standing, KE as how fast you are rolling, and EPE as how tightly a trampoline is stretched. Rolling down the hill converts height into speed, and the trampoline converts stretch into bounce. It breaks down because the speed in KE is squared, so the 'speed dial' is not linear: doubling it needs four times the energy, unlike height.
analogy.t: Energy as a hill, a speed dial and a spring

bullets: Kinetic energy: **E_k = 1/2 m v²** (joules, kilograms, metres per second).
Elastic potential energy: **E_e = 1/2 k e²** (joules, newtons per metre, metres), assuming the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
Gravitational potential energy: **E_p = m g h** (joules, kilograms, newtons per kilogram, metres).
Gravitational field strength near the Earth's surface: **g = 9.8 N/kg** (always use the value given in the question).
Learn all three equations: treat them as equations you must recall, not ones that will always be provided.
Be able to combine them, for example GPE converting to KE when something falls.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.1.1.2 (Energy changes in systems) asks you to recall and apply three equations for energy stores: the **kinetic energy** equation, the **elastic potential energy** equation and the **gravitational potential energy** equation. You must be able to substitute into them, rearrange them, and use them in problems about objects speeding up, slowing down, being lifted, dropped or stretched. Almost every Paper 1 has a 3 to 4 mark calculation using at least one of them, so accuracy with units and rearranging is worth a lot of marks.

bullets: The kinetic energy store is increased when work is done to accelerate an object; it is decreased when work is done against resistive forces (friction, braking).
Kinetic energy depends on **speed**, not velocity: it has no direction.
Because of the v², doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy **four times** bigger; tripling the speed makes it **nine times** bigger.
Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy (directly proportional to mass).
A stationary object has zero kinetic energy.
Kinetic energy is never negative because m and v² are both positive.
core.p: Anything that is moving has energy in its **kinetic energy store**. The amount depends on two things: the **mass** of the object and its **speed**. A heavier object moving at the same speed has more kinetic energy, and a faster object of the same mass has more kinetic energy. Crucially, speed has a much bigger effect than mass because the speed is **squared** in the equation. This is why high-speed crashes are far more dangerous than low-speed ones.

bullets: Step 1: write the equation, E_k = 1/2 m v².
Step 2: convert units: g to kg (divide by 1000), km/h to m/s (divide by 3.6), cm/s to m/s (divide by 100).
Step 3: square the speed, then multiply by the mass, then by 0.5.
Step 4: give the answer in joules (J), or kJ if large, with correct significant figures.
Rearranged for mass: **m = 2 E_k ÷ v²**.
Rearranged for speed: **v = √(2 E_k ÷ m)**, remembering to take the square root as the last step.
core.h: The kinetic energy equation and how to use it
core.p: The equation is **kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)²**, written E_k = 1/2 m v². The speed must be squared **first**, then multiplied by the mass and by 0.5. A very common error is to multiply mass by speed and then square the whole thing, which gives the wrong answer. Mass must be in kilograms and speed in metres per second so that the answer is in joules.

bullets: Doubling the speed from 20 to 40 m/s multiplies the kinetic energy by 4, so the braking distance (for the same braking force) is also four times as long.
The work done by the brakes equals the kinetic energy removed: F × braking distance = 1/2 m v² (for a constant force).
A heavier vehicle has more kinetic energy at the same speed, so it needs a larger braking force or distance.
The brakes heat up because the kinetic energy is transferred to their thermal store.
Speed limits are lower in built-up areas partly because of this squared relationship.
Link to Forces 4.5: stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
core.h: Why the squared speed matters: braking and safety
core.p: Because kinetic energy depends on v², small increases in speed give large increases in the energy that must be transferred away to stop a vehicle. When a car brakes, work is done by the friction force over the braking distance, so the **braking distance** needed to remove the kinetic energy is proportional to the kinetic energy, and therefore to v². This is why speeding is so dangerous and why braking distance increases much more quickly than speed. It also explains why the energy released in collisions rises sharply at high speeds, which increases injuries.

bullets: Equation: E_p = m g h (J = kg × N/kg × m).
Gravitational field strength **g = 9.8 N/kg** on Earth (the Moon is about 1.6 N/kg, so the same object has less GPE at the same height there).
Weight W = m g, so E_p = weight × height; this is just work done = force × distance.
The height is measured **vertically** from a chosen reference level; only changes in height matter in most problems.
Rearranged for height: **h = E_p ÷ (m g)**; for mass: **m = E_p ÷ (g h)**.
GPE increases when an object is lifted and decreases when it falls.
core.p: An object in a gravitational field has energy in its **gravitational potential energy store** because of its height above the ground (or above some chosen reference level). When you lift an object, work is done against the force of gravity, so the energy transferred to the store equals the weight multiplied by the vertical height. The equation is **gravitational potential energy = mass × gravitational field strength × height**, E_p = m g h. Only the **vertical height** matters, not the path taken: lifting a box straight up or along a ramp to the same height gives the same increase in the store.

bullets: Change in GPE = m g × change in height (Δh).
The energy gained by lifting comes from another store, such as the chemical store in your muscles or the electrical energy to a motor.
Falling objects convert GPE into kinetic energy (see the energy swaps section).
If the object moves along a slope, use the vertical height only.
Show the working: formula, substitution with units, answer with units.
Check size: lifting 1 kg by 1 m gives about 9.8 J, so 2940 J for a person on a ladder is reasonable.
core.h: Calculating changes in gravitational potential energy
core.p: In many questions you are asked for the **change** in gravitational potential energy, using the change in height. If a 60 kg person climbs 5.0 m up a ladder, the gain in GPE is 60 × 9.8 × 5.0 = 2940 J. If a ball drops from a table, the loss in GPE is calculated from the vertical distance fallen. Be careful to use the **vertical** distance and not the length of a slope: a 10 m ramp that rises 2 m only changes the GPE by m g × 2 m.

bullets: Equation: E_e = 1/2 k e², with k in N/m and e in m.
The **spring constant k** (N/m) tells you how stiff the spring is: a bigger k means a stiffer spring and more force needed per metre.
The **extension e** is the change in length from the natural (original) length, not the total length.
Doubling the extension makes the stored energy **four times** bigger.
Convert cm to m before using the equation (for example 15 cm = 0.15 m).
When the spring is released the elastic potential energy is transferred to the kinetic store (and some to the thermal store).
core.p: When a spring or other elastic object is stretched or compressed, work is done on it and energy is transferred to its **elastic potential energy store**. The more it is stretched, the greater the energy stored. For a spring that obeys Hooke's law, the energy stored is given by **elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)²**, E_e = 1/2 k e². This equation only works if the spring has **not been stretched beyond its limit of proportionality**, because above this limit the force is no longer proportional to the extension (and the spring may be permanently deformed).

bullets: Hooke's law: **F = k e** (force in N, spring constant in N/m, extension in m) for a linear spring.
The gradient of the force-extension graph is the **spring constant k**.
The area under the line up to a certain extension equals the energy stored, which is the work done.
For a triangle, area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × e × F = 1/2 × e × k e = 1/2 k e².
Beyond the limit of proportionality the graph curves, and you must estimate the area (for example by counting squares).
This is a good Higher-tier style reasoning route: if the line is straight, use the equation; if it curves, count the squares.
core.h: Where the 1/2 k e² comes from (Hooke's law and area under a graph)
core.p: The elastic energy equation can be understood from the force-extension graph. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, the force needed to stretch it is F = k e, so the graph of force against extension is a straight line through the origin. The work done stretching it equals the average force multiplied by the distance moved. The force goes from 0 up to k e, so the average force is 1/2 k e, and the work done is 1/2 k e × e = 1/2 k e². This is the same as the **area under the force-extension graph** (the area of a triangle).

bullets: Kinetic energy: m = 2E ÷ v², v = √(2E ÷ m).
Gravitational potential: m = E ÷ (g h), h = E ÷ (m g).
Elastic potential: k = 2E ÷ e², e = √(2E ÷ k).
Convert: 1 kg = 1000 g; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 km/h = 1/3.6 m/s (so 72 km/h = 20 m/s).
Square the whole speed or extension, including the units, before multiplying.
Give answers to a sensible number of significant figures, matching the data given (usually 2 or 3).
core.p: Exam questions rarely give you the answer in the form of the equation, so you need to be fluent with rearranging. The method is to write the equation, substitute the numbers you know, and then isolate the unknown, being careful with squares and square roots. For equations with a square, the square root is always the last step. Units matter: if you use grams or centimetres you will lose marks, and the answer may be off by a factor of 1000 or 100.

bullets: Falling: loss in GPE = gain in KE (if no air resistance).
Rising: loss in KE = gain in GPE.
Spring launching a ball: elastic potential energy → kinetic energy → GPE as it rises.
Dropped from 10 m: v = √(2 × 9.8 × 10) = √196 = 14 m/s, whatever the mass.
If air resistance acts, some energy is transferred to the thermal store, so the speed is lower than predicted.
In a closed system, the total energy is constant, so use E_total = KE + GPE + EPE at any point.
core.h: Energy swaps: GPE to KE and conservation of energy
core.p: When an object falls freely, its gravitational potential energy decreases and its kinetic energy increases by the same amount, provided air resistance is ignored. So m g h = 1/2 m v², which simplifies to **v = √(2 g h)**; the mass cancels, so all objects fall with the same speed in the absence of air resistance. This kind of question uses conservation of energy: the energy lost from one store equals the energy gained by another. The same idea applies to pendulums, roller coasters and objects thrown upwards.

bullets: Pendulum: GPE at the top, KE at the bottom, repeating; each swing is lower because of air resistance and friction at the pivot.
Bungee jump: GPE → KE → elastic potential store of the cord → back to KE and GPE as it recoils.
Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input (4.1.2), links to the dissipated energy.
Energy lost to friction goes to the thermal store of the surfaces and the surroundings.
Car braking: kinetic energy transferred to the brakes' thermal store: 1/2 m v² = F × d.
Whenever the final KE is less than the starting GPE, state the rest was dissipated as thermal energy.
core.h: Real situations: friction, air resistance and efficiency
core.p: In real life, not all the energy goes where you want it. A roller-coaster car does not reach the same height on each hill because work is done against friction and air resistance, which transfers energy to thermal stores. A bungee jumper converts gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy and then to elastic potential energy in the cord. In any calculation you should state your assumption: if the question says 'ignore air resistance' you can equate the energy changes. Otherwise the energy not accounted for is dissipated to the surroundings.

bullets: KE vs v: curve through the origin; KE vs v²: straight line through the origin with gradient 1/2 m.
GPE vs h: straight line through origin; gradient = m g = weight in newtons.
EPE vs e: curve; EPE vs e²: straight line, gradient 1/2 k.
Force vs extension (spring): straight line through origin, gradient k; area under = energy stored.
If a line does not pass through the origin, check whether the axes start at zero or the equation has an offset.
Read values carefully with the scale and include units on any answers taken from the graph.
core.p: You may be asked to recognise or sketch graphs of these energy stores. Kinetic energy against speed is a **curve** (a parabola, since E ∝ v²), starting at the origin and getting steeper. Gravitational potential energy against height is a **straight line through the origin** whose gradient is m g (the weight). Elastic energy against extension is again a curve (E ∝ e²), while force against extension is a straight line whose gradient is k and whose area gives the energy. Being able to match the equation shape to the graph is a common test of understanding.

bullets: Forces: braking distance, work done = force × distance, Hooke's law F = k e.
Energy resources: hydroelectric (GPE), wind (KE), tidal (GPE and KE).
Particle model: temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles.
Specific heat capacity: kinetic energy lost when an object is stopped is often transferred to a thermal store (ΔE = m c Δθ).
Power: P = E ÷ t; the rate at which GPE or KE is transferred.
Required practical on Hooke's law (spring) uses extension measured in metres to find k.
core.p: These equations appear across Physics. Work done by a force (4.1.1.1) is the way kinetic, gravitational and elastic energy are changed. Hooke's law and the force-extension required practical sit in the Forces topic. In Particle model, kinetic energy of particles is linked to temperature. In Electricity and Energy resources, water falling from a height in hydroelectric power uses GPE → KE → electrical energy, and wind turbines use the kinetic energy of the wind (E_k = 1/2 m v²). In Space, the orbital motion and speed of satellites use similar energy ideas.

exam: Write the equation first (1 mark), substitute with correct units (1 mark), then the answer with unit (1 mark); never skip the equation.
The answer must have a unit (J, kJ). Missing or wrong units usually lose the final mark.
Convert units before substituting: g to kg, cm to m, km/h to m/s (divide by 3.6).
For 'show that' questions, give the answer to at least one more significant figure than the question states, then round.
For 'explain why doubling the speed more than doubles the stopping distance' use: KE ∝ v², so four times the energy must be removed by the brakes.
For 'ignoring air resistance' problems, say loss in GPE = gain in KE, then use m g h = 1/2 m v².
For spring questions, check whether the spring obeys Hooke's law (the limit of proportionality is not exceeded) before using 1/2 k e².
For force-extension graphs, the gradient is k and the area under the line is the energy stored (work done).
For 6-mark answers, name the stores in order, state the equation used and say where the remaining energy goes (dissipated to the thermal store).
Command words: 'Calculate' needs working; 'Estimate' accepts rounded values; 'Explain' needs the reason (squared speed, conservation of energy).

mistakes.r: The speed only is squared: E_k = 1/2 × m × v². Square v first, then multiply.
Convert to kilograms and metres first so that the answer is in joules.
mistakes.w: Using the mass in grams or the extension in cm.

mistakes.r: KE depends on v², so doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as big.
mistakes.w: Doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy.

mistakes.r: Only the vertical height gained counts: E_p = m g h.
mistakes.w: Using the length of the slope as the height for GPE.

mistakes.r: The extension is the change in length from the natural length.
mistakes.w: Using the total length of the spring as the extension.

mistakes.r: Rearrange to v = √(2E/m) or e = √(2E/k); the square root is the final step.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the square root when finding speed or extension.

mistakes.r: Use the value of g given in the question; AQA uses 9.8 N/kg.
mistakes.w: Using g = 10 or 9.81 when the question gives 9.8.

mistakes.r: The equation only applies if the spring obeys Hooke's law; otherwise find the area under the graph.
mistakes.w: Using the equation E_e = 1/2 k e² for a spring beyond the limit of proportionality.

mistakes.r: Without air resistance v = √(2 g h), so the speed does not depend on mass.
mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster because they have more GPE.

summary: AQA 4.1.1.2 asks you to recall and use three equations: kinetic energy = 1/2 m v², gravitational potential energy = m g h (g = 9.8 N/kg) and elastic potential energy = 1/2 k e². You must substitute, rearrange and apply them, including energy swaps between stores. They feature in almost every calculation question on Paper 1.

terms.d: The energy an object has because it is moving; depends on its mass and speed.
The energy an object has because of its height above the ground in a gravitational field.
The energy stored in an elastic object when it is stretched or compressed.
The force per unit mass on an object in a gravitational field; 9.8 N/kg near the Earth's surface.
The force needed per unit extension of a spring; measured in newtons per metre (N/m).
The increase in length of a spring from its original (natural) length; measured in metres.
The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded (F = k e).
The point beyond which the extension of a spring is no longer directly proportional to the force applied.
The unit of energy; one newton metre.
The energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred, stored or dissipated.
The force acting on an object due to gravity (W = m g), measured in newtons.
Two quantities where one is a constant multiple of the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Energy that is transferred to the surroundings so that it is spread out and not useful.
The slope of a line on a graph; change in y divided by change in x.
